While the narrative is somewhat less cohesive than City Lights, Modern Times compensates with its variety and audacity. The film critiques capitalism and labor exploitation without sacrificing charm. It's a rare work that simultaneously entertains and provokes thought-highlighting worker struggles during the Great Depression with wit instead of despair.

Chaplin's restrained use of dialogue in a transitional sound era proves to be a brilliant creative choice. His expressive pantomime says more than words could, allowing the film to retain the essence of silent cinema while subtly embracing new forms.

Though nearly a century old, Modern Times is surprisingly relevant. Its themes of technological anxiety, economic hardship, and human resilience resonate as powerfully today as in 1936. Whether you're a film student, a history buff, or simply someone looking for a good laugh, Modern Times remains essential viewing. It is not just a comedy classic, it's cinematic art that speaks across generations.

Although "Modern Times" was made as late as 1936, nearly a decade after the coming of sound to the cinema, Charlie Chaplin decided to make it a "silent" as he had done with his previous film, "City Lights" from five years earlier. I place the word "silent" in inverted commas because both films make some use of sound; both, for example, have a recorded musical soundtrack. (Chaplin, a gifted musician as well as a comedian, composed this himself, as he did in a number of his films). "Modern Times" also has sound effects and a limited amount of spoken dialogue. Chaplin himself does not speak, but does sing a nonsense comic song.

There were two reasons for Chaplin's reluctance to embrace the sound revolution. Firstly, he had grown up during the silent era and had become a master of the art of silent comedy, which was very different to verbal comedy. Secondly, he wanted to make films for the whole world, not just for English-speaking ones. "Modern Times", however, was to be his last "silent"; his next film, "The Great Dictator" from 1940, was a fully-fledged talkie.

In "Modern Times" Chaplin plays his iconic Little Tramp character, now a factory worker on an assembly line. Unable to cope with the work, he suffers a nervous breakdown, and the film then chronicles a further series of misadventures. These are too many and varied for me to write a full synopsis, but the themes which run throughout the film are the Tramp's essential innocence, his inability to cope with the stresses and complexities of life in 1930s America and his love for a girl whom he meets in the course of his adventures. This girl, played by Chaplin's wife Paulette Goddard, is sometimes referred to as "Ellen", although in the cast list she is simply referred to as "a gamin". (This surprised me. I always thought that "gamin/gamine", like "blond/blonde" and "fiance/fiancee", was one of those French loan-words which always take an extra "e" in the feminine, even in English).

The most famous scenes in the film are those set in the factory, in which Chaplin satirises the production-line techniques of modern industry. On one level these scenes are highly comic, but they are also serious in that they highlight the way in which each worker's role is reduced to that of repeatedly performing a single unskilled task all day long. Management even begrudged their workforce taking time off for meals; at one point the Tramp is subjected to an experimental "automatic feeding machine", designed to do away with the need to lunch breaks by allowing workers to be fed at their posts.

Chaplin's critique of the soul-destroying effects of industrialisation led to him being attacked as a "Communist", although he was defended by Graham Greene, who stated "Chaplin presents, he doesn't offer political solutions".

Chaplin was certainly on the Left, but it is important to note that his satire was directed at the modern world in general, not just America. This was, after all, the period when many Leftists were praising Stalin for industrialising the Soviet Union, using production and management techniques borrowed from Western capitalism. Yet, although factory work may have been dehumanising, during the Great Depression people considered themselves lucky to have work of any kind, something emphasised in the film when we see a demonstration by unemployed workers. (The Tramp inadvertently gets caught up in it and is mistakenly arrested).

"Modern Times" is a difficult film to categorise. It has been described as a black comedy, a description which is apt if one takes that phrase to mean comedy with a serious edge, less so if one understands it as an attempt to get humour from cynical bad taste. It is certainly a comedy, a film in which Chaplin was able to use his finely honed silent comic skills to great effect. (Apart from the factory scenes, I loved the scene where the Tramp roller-skates on the edge of a steep drop without ever falling off, an effect achieved by the use of trompe l'oeil painting). It is also, undoubtedly, a political and social satire. Yet the Tramp is more than just a figure of fun, more than just a political symbol. He is also a recognisable human being and a symbol of our common humanity, the little man who always manages to find hope even in seemingly desperate situations. As he says at the very end of the film: "Buck up - never say die. We'll get along". 9/10.

Charlie Chaplin's Modern Times (1936) is an iconic piece of cinematic history-a satire of industrialization, a showcase of Chaplin's unmatched physical comedy, and a transitional film marking the end of the silent era. But while it's undeniably clever and ambitious, your 6/10 rating makes perfect sense for viewers who admire the artistry but don't fully connect with it emotionally or narratively.

Chaplin's Tramp, caught in the grinding cogs of a modernized society, is as agile and expressive as ever. His slapstick is pure visual poetry: fluid, inventive, and genuinely funny in moments, especially the factory scenes and the unforgettable roller-skating bit. Yet, for those not fully charmed by silent-era humor, some routines may start to feel like variations on a theme-clever, yes, but a little repetitive and emotionally distant.

The film's satire on capitalism and mechanization is sharp but not subtle. The opening scenes of the Tramp being devoured by machinery are still striking visual metaphors, but later parts lean more into episodic skits that dilute the thematic focus. The plot feels loose, wandering from factory floors to jail cells to café stages, always entertaining, but rarely cohesive or deep. There's charm, but little urgency.

Cinematographically, Modern Times is crisp and well-framed, with smart use of depth and motion. It blends silent film traditions with sound effects and a small amount of dialogue-most notably, Chaplin's iconic nonsensical "song" number, which is a standout for its creativity and cheeky commentary on the move to talkies. Still, the film sometimes feels caught between eras, and for modern audiences, the stylistic mix can come off as inconsistent.

The music, composed by Chaplin himself, is light, melodic, and emotionally attuned. The "Smile" theme, later made famous as a standalone song, adds a gentle emotional current throughout. But for all the sweet, optimistic notes, some viewers may wish for more dramatic weight or narrative payoff.

In the end, Modern Times is a film of great historical and artistic value, but its appeal largely depends on how much one connects with Chaplin's particular style. A 6/10 reflects that respectful distance: you see its brilliance, but the spark just doesn't fully ignite.

'Modern Times (1936)' is considered to be the last American 'Silent Film', made long after the era had essentially come to a close. It's fitting, then, that some use of sound seeps into the piece and usually signifies the modernisation of society, machines replacing man and bringing audio with them. It also gives us the first taste of The Tramp's voice, as he is forced into an uncomfortable situation simply to find work - though the song he sings is gibberish to keep the scene universally understandable. This picture is perhaps Chaplin's finest silent work because it not only has a message, taking a stance against the industrialisation of the workforce and its replacement by unthinking machines, but is also riotously entertaining throughout. It puts a smile on your face in the first scene and keeps it there until the last. Each slapstick set-piece comes incredibly close to brilliance, with a few easily crossing that threshold, and the feature is funny in the way only a film of this kind could be. It really is effortlessly entertaining and endlessly enjoyable, remaining a purely visual treat from beginning to end with some fantastic themes and inventive scenes. There isn't really a moment that doesn't work and the Tramp remains as endearing as ever. It's made even better because of its underlying point, one that is all the more relevant today and was actually somewhat clairvoyant, and is certainly one of the most purely cinematic pictures I've ever seen. It's a proper Chaplin classic. 8/10

Chaplin has created a movie that offers us joy even nearly ninety years after its release. And with the uplifting line from the movie I end this review - Buck up - never say die! We'll get along.

Chaplin was one of the first silent filmmakers I watched, and maybe I therefore took for granted just how good he was at the craft. His performance is great, the scenarios he crafts are great, and it's even really well shot to boot.

While the aforementioned City Lights may have a more coherent and emotional story, Modern Times has the set pieces, and surely features the highest number of memorable stand-alone sequences of any Chaplin movie.

It's wrapped up with a somewhat sudden but still very touching final scene that I think must have been intended to give the Depression-era audience hope in their own lives.
